note: 'could' is the auxiliary of an interrogative clause and 'the axis' is written as the subject of 'go', which is how 'make the axis go' reads, so the next layer can go on from here.
'stacked' is written as the verb of a nonfinite clause, which is what a lone participle is, and there is nothing else in the message for it to be tied to.
'on' ties the command to 'top' and 'of' starts at 'top', so 'top of each other' stays whole and the command keeps 'the bars' as its complement.
'I' is the subject of 'want', the 'to' relation ties 'stack' to that clause, and the 'of' relation starts at 'top' rather than at another nominal.
'would' is the auxiliary with 'stack' as the main verb in an interrogative clause, 'you' the subject, and 'top of each other' is held whole.
'just' is a modifier of the imperative clause, 'stack' its verb and 'the bars' its complement, and the 'of' relation starts at 'top', all as the words show.
'ok' is held as a word said to the listener in the imperative clause of 'stack', which matches its place in the message.

'sort he bars from smallesy to largest' is one command, but c4 writes 'bars' as the verb of a declarative clause with 'he' as its subject while 'sort' stands apart as c3, and the coordination 'so' joins the clause of 'is' with that wrong c4.

'thechart' and 'sidewaays' are written as one nominal with 'sidewaays' as its head, so the thing flipped becomes the description by which 'sideways' is found, though 'sidewaays' only says how to flip.
sop:
@c1 syntax.clause form=imperative discourse="couodyou" verb="flip" complement=$n1 modifier="sidewaays"
@n1 syntax.nominal head="thechart"
